content:
Hello everyone, I was trying to define perfect graphs and I wanted to make sure that the definition makes sense and is useful. The current definition I have is

def SimpleGraph.IsPerfect (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∀ (s : Set V), (G.induce s).chromaticNumber = (G.induce s).cliqueNum

I believe this definition is accurate and will help me towards having a prood for the weak perfect graph theorem. But I wanted to make sure it actually was, so if someone has a suggestion, they would be greatly appreciated :)

That definition looks right to me! One thing that came to mind was "how does this behave for infinite graphs", but it looks like it's correct for that, assuming that the chromatic number and clique number are finite. To expand on that:

There's a funny case where you could have a graph have infinite chromatic number, and infinite clique number. But the way cliqueNum is defined, it would give 0, not infinity. So it's possible that you would lose out on some "perfect" graphs this way.

You could imagine requiring s to be finite. Then the chromatic number and clique number are always finite, and if they diverge as s grows, their values (for infinitely large s) go to infinity as well. (I'm being a bit loose with the notion of the limit here but it checks out.) So that would be a "fix": if you want to include infinite graphs, and don't want to change the definition of cliqueNum to be an ENat, then you would want an extra assumption that s is finite.

But I don't think you should do that, because (1) almost all literature on perfect graphs is about the finite case, and (2) it complicates the definition, and (3) the "real" problem is with cliqueNum, so if someone actually wanted to work with infinite perfect graphs they should fix that first.

So I think it looks good!

You might be able to make a definition that works for the infinite case more sensible by defining a perfect graph not in terms of the numerical parameters, but instead by saying that every induced subgraph has a clique X, and a colouring c : V -> X (that is, the colours are formally the vertices of X), such that c x = x for all x in X.

This agrees with the usual definition in the finite case, and might give something less arbitrary in the infinite case. Something like the above is the right way to state Menger's theorem for infinite graphs, for example.
